extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners/agents advising on prosecution)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and evaluation of patent applications under 35 U.S.C. 112, covering the best mode requirement, enablement, definiteness (second paragraph), claim interpretation (including broadest reasonable interpretation), and means-plus-function (sixth paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what is the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what the invention is — the invention is defined in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not set forth details not relating to the essence of the invention. Unclaimed matter unrelated to the operation of the claimed invention does not trigger best mode. Case citations: In re Bosy; Northern Telecom v. Samsung; Eli Lilly v. Barr (failure to disclose unclaimed preferred mode for routine detail does not violate best mode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific example is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory requirement for the disclosure of a specific example — a patent specification is not intended nor required to be a production specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of a specific working example is not necessarily evidence that the best mode has not been disclosed, nor is presence dispositive. Best mode may be represented by a preferred range of conditions or group of reactants. (In re Gay; In re Honn.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of best mode not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are not required to point out which embodiments they consider to be their best; inclusion of the best mode contemplated by applicants is enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly labeling an embodiment as 'best' is unnecessary. (Ernsthausen v. Nakayama.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating best mode is not required for priority claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to update the best mode in foreign priority applications or in applications claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA amendments modify requirements for earlier-filed applications (disclosure must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, other than best mode). See Standard Oil Co. v. Montedison; refer to MPEP §2165 paragraph II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect in best mode cannot be cured by new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If the best mode contemplated at filing is not disclosed, the defect cannot be cured by later amendment that adds that mode as new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any proposed amendment adding a specific mode not described in the application as filed should be treated as new matter and objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 251; require cancellation of the new matter. (In re Hay.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode is distinct from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mode requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement looks to placing the claimed subject matter in the possession of the public; best mode requires disclosure of the inventor's recognized best way of practicing the invention if such existed at filing. (In re Newton; Spectra-Physics v. Coherent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume best mode disclosed absent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should assume that the best mode is disclosed in the application unless evidence is presented to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best mode rejections are extremely rare in ex parte prosecution because the necessary information is rarely accessible to the examiner and typically emerges during discovery, interference, litigation, or inter partes proceedings. Consult supervisors if contrary evidence appears. (MPEP §2165.03)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-component test for best mode rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper best mode analysis has two components: (A) whether the inventor knew of a mode they considered better than others at the time of filing (subjective); and (B) whether the disclosure is adequate to enable one skilled in the art to practice the best mode (objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only if component (A) is satisfied should component (B) be analyzed. A best mode rejection is proper only when (A) is affirmative and (B) is negative with supporting reasons. (Chemcast Corp. v. Arco Industries.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider only evidence of concealment for best mode inadequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing best mode disclosure adequacy, only evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) is to be considered — i.e., evidence that disclosure quality is so poor as to effectively result in concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of satisfied best mode include when specification delineates best mode sufficiently that only routine skill is needed, when known substitutes are available, or when the disclosed procedures produced the inventors' products. Examples of failure include concealment of non-public preferred techniques or omission of necessary steps known to inventor but not disclosed. Case examples: In re Sherwood; Honeywell v. Diamond; W.L. Gore; Scripps Clinic; Spectra-Physics; Dana Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two separate requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: The second paragraph contains two distinct requirements: (A) claims must set forth the subject matter applicants regard as their invention (subjective), and (B) claims must particularly point out and distinctly define the metes and bounds of the invention (objective/definiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first requirement depends on what applicants regard as their invention; the second is evaluated from perspective of one of ordinary skill to determine definiteness and clarity of scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for failure to claim what applicants regard as their invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is appropriate only where applicant has stated, outside the application as filed, that the invention is different from what is defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence to the contrary may appear in briefs, remarks, or affidavits (e.g., Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Prater; In re Cormany). The specification itself is not used as evidence for this requirement (In re Ehrreich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing what applicants regard as their invention is permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may change what they regard as their invention during pendency of the application; claims in continuation applications directed to originally disclosed subject matter may still receive parent filing date benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts in claimed invention during prosecution are allowable (In re Saunders; In re Brower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed essential matter (112 first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential to the invention as described in the specification may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as not enabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential matter may include missing elements, steps, or necessary structural cooperative relationships. See In re Mayhew and MPEP §2164.08(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to interrelate essential elements (112 second paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that fails to interrelate essential elements of the invention as defined by applicants in the specification may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph for failure to point out and distinctly claim the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, not all lack of interdependency between elements defeats paragraph two compliance; elements may serve independent purposes. (In re Venezia; In re Collier; Ex parte Nolden; Ex parte Huber.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (definiteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be definite to inform the public of the boundaries of protected subject matter; claims that do not meet this standard must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph as indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness rejections must clearly identify the language causing the problem and thoroughly explain the reasoning so applicant can respond by explanation or amendment. The Office emphasizes issuing patents with clear and definite claim language to enhance patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants are their own lexicographers
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may define terms in the specification and use functional language, alternative expressions, negative limitations, or any style that makes clear claim boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim may not be rejected solely because of the type of language used. If applicant sets a special meaning in the specification, that definition governs. (In re Swinehart; MPEP §2111.01.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words are given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. The specification is the best source for claim term meaning; the plain meaning presumption may be rebutted by applicant-defined definitions. BRI reduces the chance of issued claims being interpreted more broadly than justified. (In re Yamamoto; In re Zletz; In re Suitco Surface; In re Buszard.) See MPEP §2111 for full discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether each claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of claim interpretation, determine whether a limitation invokes paragraph six (means-plus-function); if so, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph six applies regardless of context (PTO examination or court proceedings). If means-plus-function is present, consult MPEP §2181(I) for determining corresponding structure and equivalents. (In re Donaldson Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether claim language is definite during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification; applicant has opportunity and duty to amend ambiguous claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During prosecution the Office uses BRI and a lower threshold of ambiguity than courts (no presumption of validity). Examiners should demand applicants resolve ambiguities so claims can be amended during prosecution rather than leaving issues for litigation. (Halliburton Energy Servs.; In re Morris; Ex parte Miyazaki.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standard for claims under examination vs issued claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Patented claims enjoy a presumption of validity and are not given BRI in courts; the PTO must construe pending claims under BRI without presumption, applying a lower threshold for ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because prosecution record is in development, applicants can explain or amend claims; the Office may reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph if, under BRI, the claim has more than one reasonable interpretation. Avoid conflating claim breadth with indefiniteness: broad is not necessarily indefinite if scope is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision for definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner's focus is whether the claim meets threshold requirements of clarity and precision, not whether more suitable language exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims are directed to such matter, allow claims that define the subject matter with reasonable particularity even if not as precise as the examiner might prefer. Examiners should suggest improved language but not reject based solely on preference. Consider: (A) content of application disclosure; (B) teachings of the prior art; (C) interpretation by one of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claim as a whole to serve notice function
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope and thus serves the notice function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The totality of limitations and their interaction must be considered. Example: a preamble may be insufficient alone but the whole claim may still satisfy notice requirements. (Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Larsen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Undeclared claim terms not indefinite if meaning discernible
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term that is not used or defined in the specification is not indefinite if the meaning of the term is discernible to one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If components of a compound term have well-recognized meanings, the reader can infer the compound meaning with reasonable confidence; thus lack of a definition in the specification does not automatically render a term indefinite. (Bancorp Services v. Hartford Life.)
